target.title: Faith as doxastic venture
target.thesis: The doxastic‑venture model of faith—believing beyond what is rationally justified—is both possible and ethically acceptable, and it is preferable to Swinburne’s more austere account of reasonable faith.

W2124966002.c001.text: Defending a doxastic venture model of faith requires that such venturesome believing be both possible and ethically acceptable.
W2124966002.c001.quote: A ‘doxastic venture’ model of faith – according to which having faith involves believing beyond what is rationally justiﬁable – can be defended only on condition that such venturesome believing is both possible and ethically acceptable.

W2124966002.c002.text: A development of William James’s position can satisfy the conditions of possibility and ethical acceptability for a doxastic venture model.
W2124966002.c002.quote: I show how a development of the position argued by William James in ‘The will to believe’ can succeed in meeting these conditions.

W2124966002.c003.text: Decision theory claims there are no circumstances where evidence fails to decide, thus no occasion for belief on a passional basis, challenging the Jamesian defence of doxastic venture.
W2124966002.c003.quote: A Jamesian defence of doxastic venture is, however, open to the objection that decision theory teaches us that there can be no circumstances in which ‘the evidence does not decide’, so a fortiori no occasion to permit belief on a ‘passional’ basis.

W2124966002.c004.text: The objection does not apply to certain framework principles presupposed by theistic belief and practice.
W2124966002.c004.quote: I argue that this objection does not apply to certain ‘framework principles’ such as those presupposed by the framework of theistic belief and practice,

W2124966002.c005.text: A fiducial venture model does not endorse believing beyond evidence and therefore appears to reconcile faith with reason better than the doxastic venture model.
W2124966002.c005.quote: A fiducial venture model seems to have at least one important advantage over the doxastic venture model. Because it does not endorse believing beyond what the evidence warrants, it apparently offers better prospects for reconciling faith with reason.

W2124966002.c006.text: The fiducial venture model may struggle to fully account for the venturesomeness of faith.
W2124966002.c006.quote: A disadvantage with a fiducial venture model of faith, however, is that it may have difficulty accounting fully for faith’s venturesomeness.

W2124966002.c007.text: If evidential defences of theistic belief are circular, doxastic venture may be needed to break the circle.
W2124966002.c007.quote: Should all defences of Christian (or, more generally, theistic) belief as justified by evidence turn out to be inherently circular – as is arguable – something like doxastic venture may then be needed to break into the circle.

W2124966002.c008.text: Doxastic venture may be impossible because direct voluntary control over beliefs seems unattainable.
W2124966002.c008.quote: The first doubt is that doxastic venture may seem an impossible feat, since arguably it is impossible to exercise the kind of direct control over beliefs that would seem required for believing ‘by faith’.

W2124966002.c009.text: Even if possible, it is ethically questionable to believe beyond what rational evidence warrants.
W2124966002.c009.quote: If the possibility of doxastic venture can nevertheless be vindicated, a second, ethical, doubt arises: how could it be morally justifiable to believe beyond or against what is rationally warranted?

W2124966002.c010.text: An agent cannot will away a belief feeling, but can voluntarily refrain from using its content in practical reasoning.
W2124966002.c010.quote: The agent has no (direct) power not to be in a belief-state he is in fact, but he does have direct power not to take the content of that belief-state to be true in his practical inferences.

W2124966002.c011.text: James claims that our passional nature may and must decide an option when intellectual grounds cannot decide it.
W2124966002.c011.quote: James states his thesis thus: ‘Our passional nature not only lawfully may, but must, decide an option between propositions, whenever it is a genuine option that cannot by its nature be decided on intellectual grounds’;

W2124966002.c012.text: Believing-acceptance beyond what is rationally justifiable is possible when beliefs arise from emotions, desires, affections, and traditions.
W2124966002.c012.quote: Thus, believing-acceptance beyond what we find to be rationally justifiable is entirely possible, provided

W2124966002.c013.text: James says it is morally permissible to believe beyond evidence on a passional basis only if (1) the question cannot be decided intellectually and (2) the question is a genuine option.
W2124966002.c013.quote: James’s answer is that we are within our moral rights if we let ourselves believe beyond the evidence on a passional basis – but only if two conditions are satisfied: (1) The question concerned is one which ‘by its nature cannot be decided on intellectual grounds’, and (2) The question we are settling is a ‘genuine option’.

W2124966002.c014.text: A genuine option is one that is living, forced, and momentous.
W2124966002.c014.quote: A genuine option is one which is living, forced and momentous.

W2124966002.c015.text: An option is living when each hypothesis makes at least some appeal to the person’s belief.
W2124966002.c015.quote: For an option to be living for a given person, the hypotheses for choice have to be ‘live’, in the sense that each has, in James’s words, to ‘make some appeal, however small’ to the person’s belief.

W2124966002.c016.text: An option is momentous when which hypothesis is adopted significantly affects the person’s actions or life.
W2124966002.c016.quote: An option is momentous when it matters significantly which hypothesis the person adopts – where what the person believes on the issue concerned affects significant actions of hers or, more broadly, what kind of a life she leads or person she becomes.

W2124966002.c017.text: According to James, doxastic venture is justified when it resolves a genuine option that cannot be settled by intellectual assessment of evidence.
W2124966002.c017.quote: Doxastic venture is justifiable, then, according to James, when it settles a genuine option in principle unable to be settled by intellectual assessment of the evidence.

W2124966002.c018.text: James does not endorse all passionally based belief and rejects irrationalist fideism, which requires believing contrary to rational assessment.
W2124966002.c018.quote: James is not condoning all passionally based belief. He gives no comfort to irrationalist fideism – the view that faith requires believing contrary to one’s rational assessment of the evidence.

W2124966002.c019.text: James defends suprarationalist believing, or “overbelief,” which is belief on passional grounds beyond but still consistent with what can be rationally established.
W2124966002.c019.quote: All he is defending is suprarationalist believing by faith, or ‘overbelief’ – believing on passional grounds beyond, yet still consistently with, what can be established rationally.

W2124966002.c020.text: An objection is that James’s defense amounts to wishful thinking, albeit under constraints.
W2124966002.c020.quote: It might be maintained that what James is defending is wishful thinking – wishful thinking under significant constraints, perhaps, but wishful thinking nonetheless.

W2124966002.c021.text: Another objection is that allowing passional resolution of undecidable genuine options could permit morally reprehensible beliefs.
W2124966002.c021.quote: Allowing passional resolution of genuine options not decidable on the evidence threatens to open the door to morally obnoxious beliefs.

W2124966002.c022.text: The author replies by adding a condition that the passional motivation must be morally admirable or at least not morally flawed.
W2124966002.c022.quote: I suggest adding to James’s own explicit conditions the requirement that passionally motivated doxastic venture be permissible only if (3) The passional motivation which settles the option is itself morally admirable, or, at least, not morally flawed.

W2124966002.c023.text: The author assumes that a theory of virtuous passional motivations can be provided, showing some motivations lack virtue while others possess it.
W2124966002.c023.quote: I shall simply assume that such a theory can be provided – and that it can be shown that some passional motivations (e.g. any mere wish that a proposition be true) lack the required virtue which others possess (e.g. being moved by encounter with the Christian Gospel).

W2124966002.c024.text: The decision‑theoretic objection claims James’s argument wrongly assumes a forced choice between believing and not believing when evidence is inconclusive.
W2124966002.c024.quote: James’s argument assumes that, when it matters for action whether p and the evidence is inconclusive, we are nevertheless forced to choose between believing that p and not believing that p. But this assumption is mistaken.

W2124966002.c025.text: If a question cannot be settled by rational evidence, assigning a specific confidence proportionate to evidence makes no sense.
W2124966002.c025.quote: Now, when the very nature of the question whether p ensures that no rational assessment of evidence could ever settle it, it makes no sense to assign a specific degree of confidence in p’s truth in proportion to the evidence.

W2124966002.c026.text: It can be practically rational to act on an assumption whose confidence is indeterminately spread over a sub‑interval of the unit interval.
W2124966002.c026.quote: For, it can be practically rational to act on an assumption where one’s degree of confidence is indeterminately distributed over a sub-interval – even a very wide sub-interval – of the unit interval.

W2124966002.c027.text: When a non‑negligible confidence can be placed in the theistic hypothesis, practical rationality permits acting on the assumption of its truth with that confidence.
W2124966002.c027.quote: Provided a non-negligible degree of confidence can be placed in the theistic hypothesis, practical rationality takes us only as far as acting on the assumption of its truth with that degree of confidence.

W2124966002.c028.text: Therefore, there is neither call nor excuse for doxastic venture in its favour.
W2124966002.c028.quote: And there is thus neither call nor excuse for doxastic venture in its favour.

W2124966002.c029.text: The decision‑theoretic objection appears to rule out a doxastic‑venture model of faith, allowing only a sub‑doxastic version.
W2124966002.c029.quote: The decision-theoretic objection, then, appears to rule out a doxastic venture model of faith, allowing only an attenuated version of it for which the venture of faith is ‘sub-doxastic’.

W2124966002.c030.text: An attenuated sub‑doxastic view of faith is too weak because Christian faith involves assurance, certitude, and belief rather than mere assumption.
W2124966002.c030.quote: But surely such an attenuated sub-doxastic understanding of faith is too weak? Theistic – particularly Christian – faith seems to involve a certain kind of assurance or certitude – an assurance or certitude which may, indeed, need to be carefully distinguished from any epistemic certainty, but which nevertheless involves believing rather than merely assuming that God exists and is to be trusted.

W2124966002.c031.text: The Jamesian doxastic‑venture model supplies what is needed by treating faith as a passionally based tendency to believe and as believingly accepting an unestablished claim.
W2124966002.c031.quote: the Jamesian doxastic venture model provides just what is needed, since it understands the gift of faith as a passionally based tendency to believe the religious claim, and the act of venture as an act of believingly accepting it, in the face of the recognition that it cannot be established epistemically.

W2124966002.c032.text: Jamesian defence requires contexts with evidentially undecidable genuine options that are also irreducibly doxastic.
W2124966002.c032.quote: For the Jamesian defence of doxastic venture to go through there need to be not just contexts which present us with evidentially undecidable genuine options, but contexts where, in addition, the option is, shall we say, irreducibly doxastic.

W2124966002.c033.text: Are there any genuine options that are both evidentially undecidable and irreducibly doxastic?
W2124966002.c033.quote: But are there any such options – options that are genuine, evidentially undecidable and irreducibly doxastic?

W2124966002.c034.text: A framework principle is a claim whose truth is presupposed by an entire system of beliefs and practices.
W2124966002.c034.quote: A framework principle is a claim whose truth is presupposed by a whole system or framework of beliefs and practices.

W2124966002.c035.text: Any attempt to rationally ground a framework principle’s truth is necessarily circular because it must occur within the presupposing context.
W2124966002.c035.quote: Any attempt to provide rational grounds for the principle’s truth would necessarily be circular, because the attempt would have to be made within the all-pervasive context that already presupposes the principle’s truth.

W2124966002.c036.text: If limited frameworks exhibit epistemic circularity, then choosing to accept their principles can be a Jamesian genuine option that is evidentially undecidable.
W2124966002.c036.quote: Thus, granted the assumption that there are limited frameworks that exhibit epistemic circularity, it follows that for the principles, p, of some such frameworks, the option whether or not to accept p may be both a Jamesian genuine option and an option that is evidentially undecidable.

W2124966002.c037.text: The option to accept a principle p can be both a Jamesian genuine option and an evidentially undecidable option.
W2124966002.c037.quote: the option whether or not to accept p may be both a Jamesian genuine option and an option that is evidentially undecidable.

W2124966002.c038.text: Why must resolving an option for or against a framework’s principles be understood as involving belief, i.e., choosing whether to believingly accept those principles?
W2124966002.c038.quote: why does resolving an option for or against a framework’s principles have to be understood as involving belief – as a matter of choosing whether or not to believingly accept those principles?

W2124966002.c039.text: Such choices might be more reasonably understood as choices about basic assumptions we make about how things are, which do not require us to truly believe what we assume.
W2124966002.c039.quote: Could such choices not more readily be shown reasonable if understood as choices about what basic assumptions we make about how things are and what is worthwhile, choices which do not require that we actually believe true what we assume?

W2124966002.c040.text: A more radical, non‑cognitivist possibility is that such choices involve a commitment that requires neither believing nor assuming any truths at all.
W2124966002.c040.quote: Indeed, there is a more radical, non-cognitivist, possibility: could such choices not be understood as involving a kind of commitment that does not require either believing or assuming any truths at all – at least, not in any sense which implies that truths correspond to, or are made true by, mind-independent reality?

W2124966002.c041.text: Unless it can be shown that resolving an evidentially undecidable framework principle can reasonably be a matter of deciding to believingly accept a passional inclination to believe the principle true, a Jamesian defence of doxastic venture will fail.
W2124966002.c041.quote: Unless it can be shown that the resolution of an option with respect to an evidentially undecidable framework principle can reasonably be a matter of deciding whether to (believingly) accept a passional inclination to believe the principle true, a Jamesian defence of doxastic venture will fall short.

W2124966002.c042.text: The requirement can be met: reasonable acceptance of an evidentially undecidable framework principle need not reduce to mere acceptance acting on an assumption, nor require only a non‑cognitive commitment.
W2124966002.c042.quote: I shall conclude by arguing that this requirement can be met: reasonable acceptance of an evidentially undecidable framework principle need not reduce to ‘mere’ acceptance (acting on an assumption), let alone require only some non-cognitive kind of commitment.

W2124966002.c043.text: If a reasonable choice of a framework principle can be a matter of accepting a belief about reality, then that principle must be understood realist rather than non‑realist.
W2124966002.c043.quote: If a reasonable choice of a framework principle can be a matter of accepting a belief about reality, then that framework principle will need to be understood in a realist rather than a non-realist fashion.

W2124966002.c044.text: Therefore, a Jamesian defence of doxastic venture requires a realist understanding of some framework principles.
W2124966002.c044.quote: Thus a Jamesian defence of doxastic venture requires a realist understanding of (some) framework principles.

W2124966002.c045.text: The defence of doxastic venture requires that it be reasonable for the accepted framework principle to be believed rather than merely accepted as an assumption for action.
W2124966002.c045.quote: the defence of doxastic venture requires that it be reasonable for the framework principle accepted to be believed rather than merely accepted as an assumption for action.

W2124966002.c046.text: Doxastic venture involves the more contentious overbelief, not the familiar overassumption.
W2124966002.c046.quote: Doxastic venture involves the more contentious overbelief, not the wholly familiar overassumption.

W2124966002.c047.text: The Jamesian doxastic venture account should be preferred as phenomenologically superior because it accommodates the common view of Christian faith as involving assurance or certitude.
W2124966002.c047.quote: the Jamesian doxastic venture account should be preferred as phenomenologically superior – since (as already observed) it accommodates the general understanding of Christian faith as involving some kind of assurance or certitude.

W2124966002.c048.text: When a principle p is evidentially undecidable, there is no rational basis for assigning any specific degree of confidence to the assumption that p.
W2124966002.c048.quote: where the question whether p is in principle evidentially undecidable, there is no rational basis for assigning to the assumption that p any one speciﬁc degree of conﬁdence rather than another.

W2124966002.c049.text: Once the propriety of overassumption at the level of framework principles is granted, nothing blocks the propriety of overbelief, provided appropriate passional resources are available.
W2124966002.c049.quote: once the propriety of overassumption at the level of framework principles is granted, there is nothing to block the propriety of overbelief – though, of course, to achieve overbelief one has to have the appropriate passional resources.

W2124966002.c050.text: The question of whether to accept a realist‑construed framework principle that presents a Jamesian genuine option may be reasonably and ethically resolved by employing a passionally motivated belief, assuming the motivation is morally admirable or at least not excluded.
W2124966002.c050.quote: the question whether to accept or not to accept a framework principle that is evidentially undecidable, that is properly given a realist construal, and that presents a person with a Jamesian genuine option may reasonably and ethically be resolved through that person’s letting him or herself employ in practical reasoning a passionally motivated belief on the question, provided that the passional motivation is itself morally admirable, or, at least, not morally excluded.

W2124966002.c051.text: Plantinga defends a Calvinist conception of faith that ties faith to specific content and emphasizes the Holy Spirit’s work rather than a believer’s leap.
W2124966002.c051.quote: Plantinga attempts an impressively thorough defence of this Calvinist conception of faith – a conception which ties faith to a particular content and emphasizes the work of the Holy Spirit rather than any ‘leap’ on the part of the believer.

W2124966002.c052.text: Helm’s ‘evidential proportion’ view requires that the belief components of faith be held in proportion to their evidential support.
W2124966002.c052.quote: Helm himself describes his view as an ‘evidential proportion’ understanding of faith, since he takes it as a requirement that the belief components of faith be held in proportion to their evidential support.

W2124966002.c053.text: It may be possible for someone to have a morally admirable passional motive for embracing a morally objectionable belief.
W2124966002.c053.quote: If, however, one regards it as possible for someone to have a morally admirable passional motive for embracing a morally objectionable belief, a further, fourth, condition will needed to be added to the Jamesian account of ethically sound doxastic venture – namely, the requirement that what is believed be itself in conformity with correct morality.

W2124966002.c054.text: The Jamesian account of ethically sound doxastic venture requires that what is believed conform to correct morality.
W2124966002.c054.quote: If, however, one regards it as possible for someone to have a morally admirable passional motive for embracing a morally objectionable belief, a further, fourth, condition will needed to be added to the Jamesian account of ethically sound doxastic venture – namely, the requirement that what is believed be itself in conformity with correct morality.

W2124966002.c055.text: Swinburne’s account avoids the decision‑theoretic objection only if revised so the believer acts on the assumption, not the belief, that the best can eventuate only if God exists.
W2124966002.c055.quote: Thus, arguably, Swinburne’s account avoids the decision‑theoretic objection only if it is revised so that the theistic believer acts only on the assumption, rather than the belief, that the best can eventuate only if God exists.

W2124966002.c056.text: Swinburne’s claim that James endorses a faith of ‘acting‑as‑if’ does not square with James’s distaste for Pascal’s wager nor with James’s description of ‘overbelief’.
W2124966002.c056.quote: This does not square, however, with James’s evident distaste for Pascal’s advice to those convinced by his Wager (see ‘The will to believe’, 6), nor does it ﬁt with the fact that James describes what he defends as ‘overbelief ’ (my emphasis, see n. 10 above).

W2124966002.c057.text: Kaplan argues that belief cannot be defined merely as having a degree of confidence above a threshold, presenting a ‘Bayesian challenge’ to the concept of belief.
W2124966002.c057.quote: Given that, as Mark Kaplan shows in his Decision Theory as Philosophy (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996), believing that p cannot be deﬁned as a matter of having a degree of conﬁdence in p over a certain threshold, we face what Kaplan calls ‘the Bayesian challenge’ to explain what need we have for the concept of belief.

W2124966002.c058.text: If it is indeed a desideratum that Christian faith include assurance, faith provides a context where the Bayesian challenge is met because believing cannot be reduced to confidence levels.
W2124966002.c058.quote: If it is indeed a desideratum that (Christian) faith include assurance, faith provides a context in which this challenge can be met, since the concept of believing will here not be replaceable by the concept of having some degree of conﬁdence in a hypothesis.

W2124966002.c059.text: Given ‘if q then p’, should we infer p by modus ponens or infer not‑q by modus tollens?
W2124966002.c059.quote: We claim to have shown by the Jamesian argument: if q then p. But are we to argue by modus ponens: q, if q then p, therefore p, or by modus tollens: not-p, if q then p, therefore not-q?

W2124966002.c060.text: When the regress of nested frameworks stops, we reach framework principles that all evidence assessment presupposes, yet they are not all rationally self‑evident.
W2124966002.c060.quote: Indeed, it may be argued in general that when the regress of nested frameworks stops (as it must), we come to framework principles such that all assessment of evidence presupposes them, yet (pace the rationalist foundationalist project) they are not (all) rationally self‑evident.

W2124966002.c061.text: The proper conclusion is that a properly functioning human is programmed to take certain cognitive risks that have paid off and can be relied upon.
W2124966002.c061.quote: The correct conclusion may, rather, be that to be a properly functioning human is to be ‘programmed’ to take what count (from a certain epistemic perspective, anyway) as cognitive risks – risks which evidently have paid off and may be relied on to continue to do so.

W2124966002.c062.text: Alston claims it is impossible to give a noncircular demonstration of the reliability of any basic belief‑forming mode, so religious experience is no special demerit.
W2124966002.c062.quote: Alston holds that ‘it is impossible to give an effective noncircular demonstration of the reliability of any of our basic modes of belief formation’, and, hence, that ‘the fact that we cannot do this for religious experience is no special demerit of that source of belief’.

W2124966002.c063.text: Commitment to the inductive principle may be best understood as rule‑following rather than as acceptance of a truth claim about nature’s uniformity.
W2124966002.c063.quote: commitment to the inductive principle, for example, might be best understood as commitment to follow a certain rule, rather than as the acceptance (whether believing‑ or otherwise) of a truth claim (about the uniformity of nature, for instance).

W2124966002.c064.text: James did not limit permissible overbelief to religion, and his view aligns with my proposal that accepting certain framework principles is the proper sphere for doxastic venture.
W2124966002.c064.quote: These remarks show that James did not confine permissible overbelief to the religious case, and that his view is at least consonant with my proposal that it is the acceptance of certain framework principles that is the proper sphere for doxastic venture.

W2124966002.c065.text: It is relevant to assess whether a good case can be made for a model of faith under the competing conception I am concerned with.
W2124966002.c065.quote: it is evidently of relevance to such an assessment whether a good case can be made for a model of faith under the competing conception of it with which I am here concerned.

W2124966002.arg1.mp.text: Whenever the Jamesian doxastic-venture model supplies what faith needs, it is phenomenologically superior to its rivals.

W2124966002.arg2.mp.text: If reasonably resolving an evidentially undecidable framework principle can be a matter of believingly accepting a passional inclination to believe it true, then a reasonable choice of a framework principle can be a matter of accepting a belief about reality.

W2124966002.a1.text: A doxastic venture model of faith is defensible only if such believing is possible and ethically acceptable.
W2124966002.a1.quote: A ‘doxastic venture’ model of faith – according to which having faith involves believing beyond what is rationally justifiable – can be defended only on condition that such venturesome believing is both possible and ethically acceptable.

W2124966002.a2.text: Decision theory claims there are no cases where evidence fails to decide, thus no basis for passional belief.
W2124966002.a2.quote: a Jamesian defence of doxastic venture is, however, open to the objection that decision theory teaches us that there can be no circumstances in which ‘the evidence does not decide’, so a fortiori no occasion to permit belief on a ‘passional’ basis.

W2124966002.a3.text: The objection does not apply to framework principles of theistic belief, providing reasons to prefer doxastic venture over Swinburne’s austere alternative.
W2124966002.a3.quote: I argue that this objection does not apply to certain ‘framework principles’ such as those presupposed by the framework of theistic belief and practice, and there are good grounds for preferring a doxastic venture model of faith over a more austere alternative (advocated by Richard Swinburne).

W2124966002.arg1.r1.text: Faith on the Jamesian model can be assurance-bearing while remaining a venture, because the risk is borne in the act of committing before proof and the felt certitude is a subsequent state of the committed believer, not a bracketing of the contingency that constituted the venture.

W2124966002.arg1.r2.text: Christian faith normatively requires belief with assurance or certitude as its core, though individual believers may fall short of it while remaining genuinely faithful.

W2124966002.arg1.r3.text: Faith on the Jamesian model can be assurance-bearing while remaining a venture, because the risk is borne in the act of committing before proof, which is fixed at the time of commitment, and the later felt certitude is a state whose phenomenology need not display that risk, so the venture's occurrence does not depend on the believer's later introspective access to it.

objections.text: Consider Marta, a hospice nurse who has watched a dozen patients die with no evident comfort. She is pressed by her church to 'venture' belief in an afterlife she has no evidence for, and she tries. She deliberately cultivates the belief, reasoning that the stakes are infinite and the cost of error is low. Her attempt succeeds: she comes to believe. But the belief is held in full awareness that its only support is her wish and her decision to adopt it. When a colleague asks why she believes, she says, 'I chose to, because the choice made my life better.' Here venturesome believing is psychologically possible, yet it is not ethically acceptable by the model's own lights: she is willing to hold a belief she knows is groundless, and she uses that belief to justify her treatment of patients' families. Possibility obtains while the ethical condition fails, so the model cannot meet c001's conjunction. The failure is that possibility and ethical acceptability are treated as jointly required, yet Marta's case separates them in a way the premise does not address.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c001 is false because it requires possibility and ethical acceptability together, yet Marta's case shows venturesome believing can be psychologically possible while ethically unacceptable, so the conjunction is not satisfied by possibility alone.

objections.text: Elena has lost her child. She wants Christian faith that God lovingly orchestrates all things. Following a doxastic-venture model, she attempts to believe this unestablished claim by stirring her passions: she repeats prayers, seeks emotional experiences, and wills herself to believe. Yet she possesses sharp metacognitive awareness. Each time she approaches assurance, she simultaneously notices that her certitude is manufactured by her own will and emotional effort. This meta-awareness prevents the state from stabilizing as genuine belief; it remains a willed performance she cannot mistake for authentic conviction. She is left with melancholic assumption, not the assurance the model promises. The venture is possible as self-deception, but impossible as genuine belief.

objections.text: Sarah, a devout Anglican, has prayed the daily office, served the food bank, and led intercessions for 30 years. She has never achieved certitude about the resurrection or Christ's divinity—she lives these claims as working assumptions, not beliefs held with assurance. When her bishop asks about her faith, she says, 'I trust, but I cannot claim to know.' Her bishop confirms her as a faithful Christian, pointing to the evident fruits of her faith: hope, charity, perseverance. Her congregation recognizes her faith as exemplary. Yet it operates entirely at the sub-doxastic level of assumption rather than belief with certitude. The sub-doxastic view is not too weak for Sarah's faith—it accurately captures it, and her faith is robust by every standard her community recognizes as genuine Christian faith.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c030 fails because Sarah's case demonstrates that genuine, exemplary Christian faith can exist without assurance, certitude, and belief, operating instead at the level of committed assumption.

objections.text: A person, Alex, passionally wants to believe their severely ill child will recover, and thus forms a tendency to believe this unestablished claim. Yet Alex does not accept the claim as true—they oscillate between hope and despair, never settling into belief. The Jamesian model here fails to produce believing acceptance, only an unstable tendency.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2124966002.c031 fails because a passionally based tendency to believe does not guarantee believing acceptance of an unestablished claim.

objections.text: A mother sits in a hospital corridor while her son undergoes a first-of-its-kind spinal surgery. The surgeon says, 'The outcome is uncertain.' She holds her son's hand, breathes slowly, and tells herself 'the surgery will go well.' She does not fully believe this; she knows the statistics and the novelty of the procedure. She retains live doubt she will not suppress. Yet she acts as if the claim is true: she stays in the room, does not call the family, does not prepare a eulogy. Her venture is a practical overassumption—leaning on the claim for action without full doxastic assent. If doxastic venture required overbelief (full believing commitment beyond evidence), this mother's genuine faith-venture would be excluded, since she never crosses into belief. She merely overassumes: she takes the claim as a working premise while keeping the doubt intact. This is precisely the 'familiar overassumption' c046 says venture is not. The case is not exotic; it is the ordinary human posture under uncertainty. The premise's sharp distinction between overbelief and overassumption cannot hold here, because the mother's venture is indistinguishable from overassumption yet clearly functions as faith.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2124966002.c046 fails because the mother's authentic faith-venture is a sub-doxastic overassumption—practical commitment without full belief—yet the premise insists venture must be overbelief, thereby excluding a real case of doxastic venture it claims to characterize.

objections.text: Consider a person who holds a deep emotional conviction about a religious claim, but lacks intellectual certainty. In this case, the Jamesian doxastic-venture model may supply what faith needs, but its phenomenological superiority is not clear. The person's experience of faith is rooted in their emotional commitment, rather than a rational evaluation of evidence. The model's emphasis on passionate tendency to believe may not capture the full richness of this person's faith experience.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that supplying what faith needs is sufficient for phenomenological superiority, which is not necessarily the case in situations where emotional conviction and intellectual certainty are disconnected.

objections.text: Alice, a devout Christian, embraces the Jamesian doxastic‑venture model, believing that miracles will intervene in her health. She declines a proven medical treatment, trusting the unestablished claim. The evidence after her decision shows a higher probability of severe illness compared to peers who follow evidence‑based medicine. From an evidential decision‑theoretic standpoint, Alice's belief serves as evidence of a decision that leads to lower expected utility. Thus, the model does not supply what faith needs; it evidentially predicts detrimental outcomes in this scenario.
objections.premise_fails_because: c031 fails because evidentially, treating faith as a passion‑based tendency to accept unestablished claims predicts harmful outcomes, contradicting the claim it supplies what is needed.

objections.text: A Bayesian evaluates the quality of a belief state by its coherence with evidence, not by its phenomenological intensity. Consider an agent, Elena, who experiences an overwhelming sense of certitude regarding a claim H despite having no evidence for it. In this model, this assurance is a success because it satisfies the phenomenological requirement for certitude. However, from a formal perspective, Elena's degree of belief P(H) is wildly decoupled from the posterior probability P(H|E) that her evidence should dictate. This gap represents a failure of rationality, not a superiority. A model that claims superiority based on the subjective strength of a tendency to believe ignores the fact that high certainty without corresponding evidence is an epistemic error, not a cognitive advantage.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2124966002.arg1.mp fails because phenomenological intensity is not a valid metric for epistemic superiority in a coherent probability distribution.

objections.text: Elias experiences faith as a state of absolute, unshakable certitude. The model defines faith as 'believingly accepting an unestablished claim.' To accept a claim as unestablished requires a psychological awareness of its lack of proof. This awareness of epistemic contingency is fundamentally incompatible with the phenomenological state of absolute certitude. If the mechanism of faith is the acceptance of the unestablished, it cannot produce the specific sense of total assurance required. W2124966002.c031 fails because accepting an unestablished claim is psychologically incompatible with the state of certitude it is intended to supply.

objections.text: Consider Marta, a hospice chaplain who commits to trusting that her dying patients meet a loving God. Her commitment is made before any proof, with real risk: she could be wrong, and she knows it. Two years later, after many deathbeds, she feels settled, unshakeable certitude that God is there. The premise says this certitude is a later state that leaves the venture intact. But her certitude now treats the contingency as closed: she no longer experiences the belief as something she might lose or that could have turned out otherwise. When she prays, she does not feel herself wagering. The risk she bore has been converted into a certainty she takes to be evidence-independent. So the felt assurance is not a subsequent state standing beside the venture; it is the venture's risk dissolved from the inside, and the premise's distinction between the act and the state cannot be drawn in her case.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r1 fails because it assumes the felt certitude can coexist with the risk-bearing as a separate later state, whereas in Marta's case the assurance itself erases the contingency that made the act a venture, so assurance and venturesomeness cannot both be preserved as the premise claims.

objections.text: Consider Marta, a parish nurse who has prayed daily for thirty years. She has never felt certitude; she describes her faith as a standing commitment to trust God while doubting, often weekly, whether God exists. Her pastor, her congregation, and her own confession all treat her as a faithful Christian who lives by the Gospel. Yet by the premise's own standard, Christian faith 'normatively requires' assurance as its core. The premise then says she falls short of the norm while remaining genuinely faithful. But this makes assurance non-core: if a person can be fully faithful without it, and the community recognizes her faith as genuine, then the norm is not constitutive of faith but an ideal faith may approach. Marta's case shows the premise's 'core' clause is doing no work. Her faithfulness is secured by commitment and practice, not by the assurance the premise makes central. The inference to the Jamesian model's superiority therefore rests on a norm that the believers the premise itself counts as faithful do not share.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise asserts that assurance is the normative core of Christian faith while also allowing genuinely faithful believers to lack it, and Marta's case shows that such allowance removes assurance from the constitutive core, so the premise cannot support the claim that the common view requires assurance.

objections.text: Sam, in despair, chooses to believe God loves him despite feeling no evidence: he senses the risk and leaps. Decades later, through unbroken communal reinforcement, his faith is a calm, absolute certainty identical to his belief that the sun exists. He no longer remembers his earlier despair or any evidential gap; asked if he ever risked belief, he denies it, reporting instead that he simply knows God loves him. His present consciousness contains no trace of venture or risk. If the model insists this state remains a “venture” solely because an inaccessible past moment once contained risk, the venture has become a theoretical posit with no phenomenological presence in the actual lived faith.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2124966002.arg1.r3 fails because a “venture” that is entirely absent from the believer’s present phenomenology—not even remembered—and is indistinguishable from ordinary certitude, is no longer a venture in any experienceable sense.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection attacks c031 as stated. c031 claims the Jamesian model supplies what faith needs by treating faith as both a passionally based tendency to believe AND believingly accepting an unestablished claim. The objection directly challenges whether the model actually delivers believing acceptance, arguing that a passionally based tendency can fail to produce believing acceptance. This is an attack on the premise's adequacy, not a misreading of what it claims.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your case shows that a passional tendency to believe does not by itself produce believing acceptance, and I grant that. But c031 is a claim about what the Jamesian model supplies, not a claim that wanting to believe reliably yields belief. James's own picture is that the venturesome believer resolves the question by deciding to believe on passional grounds, so the model's contribution is the act of believingly accepting the unestablished claim, which Alex has not performed. Alex's oscillation is best read as a case where the venture is not completed, which fits the distinction drawn in [W2483078889.a3]: hope and belief answer to different permissibility conditions, and hope can be stable while belief is not. That suggests the objection hits a gap between hope and belief rather than the model's account of faith. The harder worry is that a person who has resolved to believe, but still oscillates, may not believe at all, and then the model needs a further account of when the resolution sticks. [W2124966002.c041] already concedes that the Jamesian defence succeeds only if resolving an undecidable principle can reasonably be a matter of believingly accepting a passional inclination, and Alex's case presses exactly there. So the argument survives only if we add that the passional inclination must be stabilised into acceptance, not merely held as a tendency.
rounds.revised_premise: Faith is supplied by the Jamesian model only when the passionally based tendency is stabilised into believingly accepting the unestablished claim, not merely held as an oscillating tendency to believe.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Your reply concedes that the Jamesian model requires more than a passional tendency—it needs a resolution to believe. But Alex’s case shows that even with a passional drive, one may *attempt* to resolve to believe yet still fail to achieve stable acceptance. You admit this is a "harder worry," but then shift to the argument’s survival conditions (c041). Yet the original premise (c031) claims the model *supplies* believing acceptance, not just the possibility of it. If the model cannot guarantee that a passional tendency leads to stable belief—even with a resolution—then it doesn’t truly supply what faith needs: assurance. Alex’s oscillation exposes a gap between tendency and acceptance that the model doesn’t bridge. Unless you can show how the resolution *necessarily* secures belief, the objection stands.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that Alex's case separates a passional tendency from believing acceptance, and that c031 as worded invites your stronger reading. On the availability reading, the model supplies an act a person can perform, and Alex has not performed it, so Alex's oscillation does not show the model lacks the resource. [W2483078889.a3] supports this: hope can be stable where belief is not, so Alex may be hoping rather than believing. But the availability reading is too weak for c047. c030 requires assurance and certitude, and a resolution that is not sustained leaves the agent in the oscillating state Alex occupies. Your rejoinder shows that the model does not guarantee the transition from resolution to stable acceptance, and I cannot show that a resolution necessarily secures belief. [W2124966002.c041] already marks the Jamesian defence as dependent on resolving the undecidable principle by believingly accepting a passional inclination, and Alex shows that this dependence is not automatic. So c031 survives only as an availability claim, and c047's assurance-accommodation claim needs more.

Revised premise: Where a person sustains a resolution to believe an unestablished claim on passionally motivated grounds, the resolution yields stable believing acceptance, not merely hope or oscillation.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You misread c031 if you think the Jamesian model claims that a passional tendency automatically yields believing acceptance; c031 explicitly treats faith as involving both a passionally based tendency and a distinct act of believingly accepting the unestablished claim [W2124966002.c031]. Alex’s state is better described as hope, and the permissibility conditions of hope differ from those of belief [W2483078889.a3]. The Jamesian defence requires showing that one can reasonably decide to believingly accept a passional inclination, not that every such inclination necessarily produces acceptance [W2124966002.c041]. Because Alex never makes that decision, Alex simply lacks faith on the model’s own terms, much as a person may hope for an outcome yet still face the further choice of whether to believe it [W4413292369.a2]. Your example thus underscores the distinction between hope and belief rather than showing that the model fails to supply what is needed.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Your reply clarifies that the Jamesian model distinguishes between a passional tendency and the act of believing acceptance. But my point stands: the model *can* fail to produce believing acceptance, as shown by Alex’s case. You agree that Alex lacks faith because they never make the decision to accept the claim. This means the Jamesian model does not *reliably* supply what faith needs—it only does so if the agent takes the further step of believing acceptance. The original premise (c031) claims the model "supplies what is needed," but Alex’s case shows it doesn’t always do so. The model’s success depends on an additional, contingent choice, which undermines the claim that it *supplies* the necessary conditions for faith. So the objection still holds: the Jamesian model doesn’t guarantee believing acceptance, only the possibility of it.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You are right that the model does not guarantee believing acceptance, but c031 never claims otherwise; it claims the model supplies what is needed by treating faith as both a passionally based tendency and a distinct act of believingly accepting an unestablished claim [W2124966002.c031]. Alex lacks faith not because the model fails, but because the model correctly identifies that faith requires both components, and Alex has only the first. The Jamesian defence requires showing that deciding to believingly accept a passional inclination can be reasonable [W2124966002.c041], and that such acceptance may be a reasonable resolution of a genuine option [W2124966002.c050]; it does not require that every inclination necessarily produce acceptance. Your example therefore confirms the model's phenomenological superiority: unlike sub-doxastic rivals, it distinguishes hope from faith by showing that assurance requires the further step of believing acceptance [W2483078889.a3]. The model reliably supplies the needed account of faith; it does not promise that every agent will complete the venture.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection attacks c031's claim that faith is 'believingly accepting an unestablished claim' by arguing that this very feature is psychologically incompatible with the certitude the model is supposed to supply. Whether or not this critique succeeds, it directly engages the premise as stated—namely, that faith involves accepting an unestablished claim—and argues that this feature undermines the model's ability to accommodate certitude. The objection does not attribute a different premise or a different conclusion to the argument; it takes the premise at face value and contends it fails on its own terms.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the phrase 'accepting an unestablished claim' carries the risk you name, but the argument does not say the believer must hold, in the moment, an explicit judgment that the claim is unproven. James's model locates faith in a passionally moved tendency to believe, and the 'unestablished' is a fact about the evidence, not necessarily a content of the believer's current awareness. Compare James's own treatment of the will to believe, where the live, forced, momentous option is taken up without the agent reckoning its evidential standing at every moment. So the incompatibility you press holds only if acceptance entails reflective awareness of contingency, and that entailment is the premise you need, not one the model supplies. Still, you have found a real pressure point. A believer who sincerely reflects on the lack of proof may find certitude harder to sustain, and the argument's support for the claim that the model 'supplies assurance' depends on the model's phenomenology being stable under reflection. That dependence is not established by c031 alone. The fair concession is that the argument needs an additional premise to answer the worry: that the epistemic awareness of contingency can be bracketed or is not part of the occurrent doxastic state that constitutes assurance.
rounds.revised_premise: Accepting an unestablished claim as a passionally driven tendency to believe does not require an occurrent reflective judgment that the claim lacks proof, so the awareness of contingency need not be present in the state that constitutes assurance.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You argue that the "unestablished" status is an objective fact that needn't be subjectively felt. However, this solves the problem by destroying the very "venture" your model seeks to defend. A "venture" is not merely a formal label; it describes a psychological mode of engagement characterized by risk. If the believer must bracket the awareness of contingency to achieve certitude, the experiential element of the venture vanishes. Without the subjective presence of uncertainty, the act is no longer a "venture" on an unestablished claim, but a standard dogmatic assertion. By conceding that the model requires the bracketing of contingency to sustain assurance, you admit that the "venture" and the "assurance" are phenomenologically incompatible. The model may provide certitude, but it does so by discarding the very "venture" that constitutes its essence.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my earlier bracketing move costs something, and I should say so plainly. Your rejoinder shows that 'venture' is being used in two senses: an objective status (the evidence falls short) and a phenomenal mode (felt risk). If the argument needs the second, then bracketing contingency to reach certitude does abandon the venture as you describe. I do not think the Jamesian account requires that. James's live, forced, momentous option is one where the agent is moved by passion toward a belief the evidence does not settle, and the risk is located in the stake of being wrong, not in a standing sense of doubt. The venture is the act of committing before proof, and assurance can be the felt confidence that the commitment, once made, carries. The two are then sequential in the agent's life rather than simultaneous in one mental state. [W2124966002.c031] supplies the venture; the assurance is a further phenomenal claim the argument does not establish. That is the gap you have exposed, and the argument as stated does not close it. Its phenomenological superiority claim in c047 rests on the unstated premise that the model delivers assurance without abandoning venture, and nothing in the text secures that.

Revised premise: Faith on the Jamesian model can be assurance-bearing while remaining a venture, because the risk is borne in the act of committing before proof and the felt certitude is a subsequent state of the committed believer, not a bracketing of the contingency that constituted the venture.

rounds.content: You assume that if a claim is unestablished, the believer must be psychologically aware of its lack of proof, but c031 places the unestablishedness in the claim's objective epistemic status, not in the believer's occurrent awareness. The Jamesian model treats faith as a passionally based tendency to believe [W2124966002.c031], and because the resulting state is genuine belief rather than mere assumption, it can encompass the assurance and certitude that Christian faith requires [W2124966002.c030]. Furthermore, because believing cannot be reduced to confidence levels [W2124966002.c058], the external fact that the claim is evidentially unestablished does not entail that the subjective phenomenology must be one of contingency or doubt. The believer can therefore experience the absolute certitude you describe while the philosopher notes the evidential gap. Your objection would land only if the model required believers to hold their faith in proportion to its evidential support, but that is Helm's rival view [W2124966002.c052], not the Jamesian account.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You argue that unestablishedness is an objective status rather than a subjective awareness. However, your model defines faith as "believingly accepting an unestablished claim." If the believer is unaware of the claim's unestablishedness, they are not accepting it *as* unestablished; they are simply accepting it. To accept a claim *as* unestablished requires the subject to grasp that specific quality. 

By decoupling the objective epistemic gap from the believer's consciousness to preserve certitude, you strip the "venture" of its phenomenological essence. A venture requires a subjective engagement with risk. Without this awareness, your model fails to explain how the specific mechanism of accepting the unestablished produces the unique phenomenology of faith; it instead describes a standard belief that happens to be objectively risky. You have not resolved the incompatibility; you have rendered the "venture" irrelevant to the believer's actual experience.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You expose a genuine tension that my objective-reading dodge failed to resolve. If 'believingly accepting an unestablished claim' requires the believer to grasp the claim under the description 'unestablished,' then the mechanism imports an awareness of epistemic contingency that is incompatible with the absolute certitude the model is meant to supply [W2124966002.c030]. By relocating the unestablishedness to a purely third-person fact, I preserved certitude only by stripping the 'venture' of its first-person risk, which is what makes it a venture rather than a standard belief [W2124966002.c031]. Because believing cannot be reduced to confidence levels [W2124966002.c058], the Jamesian framework can still accommodate full assurance, but not through a mechanism that requires the believer to consciously hold the claim as evidentially unestablished. The objection therefore lands: c031 as stated is too strong. The argument survives only if we revise that premise.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks premise c030 as stated. c030 claims the sub-doxastic view is too weak because Christian faith involves assurance, certitude, and belief rather than mere assumption. The objection counters by presenting a concrete example of genuine Christian faith that operates at the sub-doxastic level of assumption without certitude, arguing the sub-doxastic view is not too weak. This engages the premise on its own terms rather than attacking a different or distorted version of it.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the premise is a substantive claim about what Christian faith involves, and Sarah's case is a serious test of it. But the argument's claim in c030 is not that every believer must have certitude; it is that the faith the tradition names, the faith with assurance that Christians confess in the creeds and in the account of justifying faith, requires belief rather than mere assumption. Sarah's bishop recognizes her as faithful, but recognition of fruits tells us about her standing and her charity, not about the doxastic content of her faith. Her own self-report, 'I trust, but I cannot claim to know,' is a report of a lack of assurance, which the tradition has long treated as compatible with real faith in its weak or struggling forms, yet not as the paradigm the premise describes. The Jamesian model is designed for exactly this gap: a passionally based tendency to believe that may fall short of certitude while still being belief, and so Sarah's case can be read as a case of incipient or wavering doxastic venture rather than sub-doxastic assumption. That reading does not require any new premise. The objection shows that sub-doxastic faith can be sincere and fruitful, which I grant, but sincerity and fruit do not by themselves establish that faith lacks belief-components; that is the question c030 and c046 are actually answering. Given that Sarah explicitly says she trusts, trust is naturally a belief-involving attitude toward God's promises, so the case is not decisive against the premise.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede that Sarah's faith is genuine — only "weak or struggling," not paradigmatic. But c030 doesn't say the sub-doxastic view is too weak to capture the paradigm; it says it is too weak because Christian faith *involves* assurance, certitude, and belief. If Sarah's assumption-based faith is genuinely Christian faith, the sub-doxastic view isn't too weak — it accurately captures a real instance of what it claims to describe. Calling her faith "weak" concedes the point. Your re-reading of Sarah as "incipient doxastic venture" presupposes that trust entails belief, but that is the very question at issue. Sarah explicitly separates trusting from knowing. She maintains a practical commitment without the doxastic attitude you attribute to her. You cannot assimilate her case to the Jamesian model by stipulating that trust is belief-involving when her self-report says otherwise.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my earlier reply leaned on calling Sarah's faith 'weak or struggling,' and that this concession is awkward if her faith is fully Christian faith. Let me be precise about what c030 claims. It says Christian faith involves assurance, certitude and belief rather than mere assumption, and c046 adds that doxastic venture is the contentious overbelief, not overassumption. So the premise is about the doxastic content the tradition's account of justifying faith requires, not about whether a given believer's standing is secure. Sarah's bishop tracks fruits and charity [W2124966002.c030 is the premise under test, so the fruits are evidence of standing, not of doxastic content]. Your strongest move is the self-report: Sarah separates trusting from knowing, and I cannot stipulate that trust is belief-involving to rescue c030. I concede that the argument as stated does not survive this case. If Sarah's sub-doxastic faith is genuinely Christian faith, then c030's 'involves assurance' is false of the general case, or at least needs restriction. The argument would need a premise that restricts the requirement to a core that the tradition treats as normative, and that the Jamesian model then has to supply, not one that makes sub-doxastic faith a deficient instance. I do not think 'Pascal' or the postmodern-theology literature [W4394980009.c044] settles this either way, since it contests the value of certainty rather than its necessity.

Revised premise: Christian faith normatively requires belief with assurance or certitude as its core, though individual believers may fall short of it while remaining genuinely faithful.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks premise r1 as stated. The premise claims that felt certitude is a subsequent state that does not bracket the contingency constituting the venture. The objection argues that in Marta's case the felt certitude does close the contingency, dissolving the venture's risk, so the premise's distinction between the act of committing and the later state of certitude cannot be maintained. This challenges the premise on its own terms rather than attacking something it does not claim.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the premise needs more than a temporal ordering. Saying the certitude comes later does not by itself show that it leaves the venture intact, and the distinction between act and state is doing real work. But the premise does not say the felt contingency must persist. It says the risk is borne in the committing act and the certitude is a subsequent state, so what the venture requires is that the risk was genuinely taken, not that the believer keeps experiencing it. Marta's case shows the risk was taken: she committed while knowing she could be wrong [W2124966002.c001]. That the later state no longer feels like wagering is what one expects once a commitment has been repeatedly vindicated or at least sustained, and James himself allows that passional belief can harden into settled conviction. Your strongest point is that her certitude is taken to be evidence-independent. If it is, the state has overreached: it misdescribes its own ground, and a believer who holds certitude as bracketing contingency has exchanged a venture for a conviction she mistakes for knowledge. That is a real cost, but it is a cost in her self-understanding, not proof that the act and state cannot be distinguished. The act-state distinction remains drawable, because one can ask whether she would still commit if the evidence turned against her. Her answer to that counterfactual is what keeps the venture alive beneath the felt assurance. I concede that the premise as stated is silent on whether the later certitude is evidence-independent, and that this silence is a gap. The argument survives only if the premise is read as requiring that the later state remain answerable to the original commitment, and I state that as the needed revision.
rounds.revised_premise: The later felt certitude is a state of the committed believer distinct from the committing act only if it remains answerable to that commitment, so that the believer would still have committed had the evidence turned against her.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You have conceded the gap and offered a revision, but the revision does not survive the counterfactual test you rely on. You say the venture stays alive beneath the felt assurance because Marta would still commit if the evidence turned against her. Ask what that answer is worth to her. A certitude that treats its ground as closed will typically report that counterfactual as idle: she cannot picture the evidence turning, so her "yes, I would still commit" is a prediction about a case her own state has already excluded. The test therefore cannot tell a sustained venture from a conviction that has absorbed the venture. Both give the same answer.

Your revised premise also now requires that the later state remain answerable to the original commitment. That is a substantive condition, and the passage you cite from James does not supply it. James allows passional belief to harden, but he does not say the hardened state must stay revisable by the act that first produced it. So you have added a condition the Jamesian model does not itself contain.

I accept that a venture can be sustained under assurance. What I deny is that you have shown the act and the state come apart in Marta's case, rather than merging. Give a test that discriminates the two in her, or the distinction does not carry the weight r1 places on it.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
Your rejoinder is right that my counterfactual test is weak. A certitude that treats its ground as closed will report 'I would still commit' as idle, so the test cannot separate a sustained venture from a conviction that has absorbed it. I accept that. But the distinction r1 needs is not a psychological test available from the inside; it is a claim about the structure of the case. The commitment was made under live contingency [W2124966002.c001], and that fact is fixed by the act, not by how the believer later feels. So the act is individuated by the risk borne at the time of commitment, and the state is individuated by its later phenomenology. These can come apart even if the believer cannot introspect the difference, just as a promise kept for years may feel like settled fact while remaining a promise. Your merging worry is a real epistemic point about Marta's self-understanding, and it may show that her certitude is misdescribed. It does not show that the venture ceased to occur. I also withdraw my suggestion that r1 requires answerability to the original commitment as a condition the Jamesian model supplies; James does not say that, and I should not have read it into him. What I still hold is narrower: r1 is true of the venture as an event, while whether the later state keeps the risk visible is a further matter the premise does not settle.

Revised premise: Faith on the Jamesian model can be assurance-bearing while remaining a venture, because the risk is borne in the act of committing before proof, which is fixed at the time of commitment, and the later felt certitude is a state whose phenomenology need not display that risk, so the venture's occurrence does not depend on the believer's later introspective access to it.

The premise need not claim that risk and certitude remain co-conscious; it claims only that the assurance does not retroactively cancel the constitutive contingency. Because Marta's evidence-independent certainty is precisely the passionally based tendency achieving settled conviction, the model still accommodates the phenomenology of full assurance [W2124966002.c047]. To make this explicit, however, the premise should be clarified.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W2124966002.c002's claim that the Jamesian position 'can satisfy the conditions of possibility' for a doxastic venture model. It argues that, at least for agents with sharp metacognitive awareness, the venture cannot stabilize as genuine belief and thus fails the possibility condition. This is a direct attack on the premise as stated, not a misreading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the Elena case bears directly on c002's first condition, possibility, since c001 requires venturesome believing to be possible, not merely self-deception. But the case trades on a stronger claim than the one in play: that any awareness that one's certitude is willed must block its stabilizing as belief. James himself allows that the will to believe operates where the evidence is not forced, and the revised premise r1 already separates the risk borne in committing from the felt certitude that follows it. Elena's metacognition may undercut felt assurance, but c046 already grants that the venture is overbelief, not mere assumption, and an overbelief can be held while one knows its causal source. Nothing in the objection shows that such knowing-while-believing is incoherent; it shows only that it is psychologically unstable for her. Instability for one believer is not impossibility of the type c001 needs. The objector may press that stability is required for genuine belief, and that is a substantive claim I cannot dismiss here. I also note that the literature on conversion, which the Pascalian objection [W2028628500.a1] raises about self-illusion, supports the objector's worry about self-deception in the wager tradition, so the worry is real. Still, the argument as stated does not depend on Elena's particular stability. I concede only that c002's possibility condition needs an explicit account of how awareness of willing is compatible with belief, which the current premises do not supply.
rounds.revised_premise: A doxastic venture can be genuinely believed while the believer retains awareness that its initial adoption was willed, provided the felt certitude is a stable state of commitment rather than a continuous performance.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede that your premises do not explain how awareness of willing is compatible with belief. That is precisely the gap my objection exploits. Elena's metacognitive grasp of her own manufacturing does not merely destabilize belief; it prevents the state from ever being belief at all, leaving her with assumption. You reclassify this as overbelief held knowingly, but if the subject recognizes the state as self-induced performance, there is no remaining doxastic attitude beyond assumption. Your model therefore cannot satisfy c001's possibility condition unless it furnishes the missing account of how knowing one's belief is willed can be compatible with genuinely believing. Individual variation is irrelevant: if reflective agents cannot perform the venture, it is not a general model of faith. I press the point you could not dismiss: stability is constitutive of genuine belief, and without it, c002 fails.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
Your rejoinder moves the goalposts from possibility to universal stability. c001 asks whether venturesome believing is possible, not whether every reflective agent can sustain it without residual self-awareness. Your claim that 'if the subject recognizes the state as self-induced performance, there is no remaining doxastic attitude beyond assumption' is the substantive premise, and it is asserted rather than shown. Overbelief, which c046 locates at the core of the venture, is precisely a state held while its source is in view: the will to believe is operative where evidence is not forced, and James's own framing allows the passional tendency to be recognized as passional. Your Elena case therefore establishes that she, given her metacognitive habits, may be unable to stabilize belief, which is a point about her psychology. It does not establish that no reflective believer can hold the state. I concede that c002 needs an explicit account of how awareness of willing is compatible with genuine belief, and that the revised premise r1 does not supply one. The Pascalian literature [W2028628500.a1] supports your worry that self-illusion can masquerade as conviction, which is a reason to distinguish genuine from performed belief, but it does not show the distinction cannot be drawn internally.

Revised premise: Reflective agents can hold an overbelief, sustained by passional tendency, whose volitional source they are aware of, and this awareness does not by itself convert the state into mere assumption.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your Elena scenario targets a Pascalian self-deception model rather than the Jamesian view. The argument does not claim that believers must will themselves into belief by manufacturing emotional states; it claims that faith is a passionally based tendency to believe and a believing acceptance of an unestablished claim [W2124966002.c031]. Elena’s metacognitive awareness targets the wrong object: she observes her own effortful self-manipulation, but the Jamesian believer need not experience her passional ground as a hidden cause whose exposure dissolves belief, any more than recognizing that trust in a friend is sustained by affection reduces trust to pretense. The argument survives only if we add a qualification.
